heading: PROPHET IBRĀHĪM (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ)
title: THE COURAGE OF FAITH
themes: Tawḥīd • Courage • Trust • Mercy • Family • Worship
scope: 12 connected fictional Imaan & Akhlaq stories | 16 Qurʾān-linked learning missions | 16 daily actions
reviewNote: Scholarly review, Arabic proofing, accessibility and safeguarding approval required before publication.
introduction: Volume Six continues the five completed ʿIBRAH Junior worlds on Ādam, Idrīs, Nūḥ, Hūd and Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon them). Prophet Ibrāhīm (AS) deserves a fuller treatment because the Qurʾān presents numerous connected episodes: his call to Tawḥīd; dialogue with his father; challenge to celestial and idol worship; the fire; the debate with a ruler; questions and reassurance; migration; the family of Ḥājar and Ismāʿīl; hospitality and glad tidings; the great test; and raising the foundations of the Kaʿbah.

The earlier children’s manuscript “Ibrahim AS.docx” contains eleven suspenseful episodes about a compass and attempts to imagine the children travelling into the past. This working edition respectfully retains its eleven thematic movements and the compass mystery, then adds a twelfth closing episode. The narrative device has been changed: children explore original sources through an ordinary library compass, cards, and modern scenarios. We deliberately do not present time travel, direct encounters with Prophets, or invented speech of Ibn Kathīr as sacred history. The existing adult ʿIBRAH Volume Six outline of twenty-four research units informs the source scope; this document is a children’s adaptation, not a claim that all adult units are reproduced verbatim.

stories.title: The Compass That Asked a Question
stories.subtitle: The library mystery begins; learning to seek the One Creator

blocks.text: The old book landed on the carpet with a thump. Akhlaq insisted that it had moved by itself. Imaan, who had seen his elbow catch the shelf, was not persuaded. Before either could settle the argument, Sheikh Uncle appeared from behind a row of books. He looked at the fallen volume, then at the two children, and quietly asked, ‘Which of you will tell me what happened?’ Akhlaq sighed. ‘My elbow knocked it down.’ Imaan helped him lift it. That small admission, Sheikh Uncle said, was already a useful beginning for a journey about truth.

Behind the book was a narrow wooden case, carefully wrapped in brown paper. Sheikh Uncle opened it and laid a brass compass on the table. It had no map of north or south. Around its edge were twelve engraved marks. Inside the lid were three words: SEE. REMEMBER. RETURN. Akhlaq turned it over, hoping to discover batteries or a secret switch, but found nothing. ‘Does it really point to something?’ he asked. ‘To a question,’ Sheikh Uncle replied. ‘Not to a city. Not to treasure. To the question you should ask when something impressive distracts you from what is true.’

A folded sheet listed the first journey: the life of Prophet Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. Dadi Jaan joined them and reminded the children that the Qur’an praises Ibrāhīm's sound guidance even before recounting many of his arguments. His people had become attached to things they fashioned and inherited. They relied on objects that could neither create nor independently benefit them. Ibrāhīm called them to worship Allah alone. ‘The objects were visible,’ said Imaan, ‘but their being visible did not make them worthy of worship.’

To test the point, Sheikh Uncle placed a model windmill, a clock and a handmade toy boat on the table. Akhlaq admired the clockwork and asked who built it. He admired the boat and asked who designed it. Dadi Jaan asked him why he was so quick to praise the maker of a toy but sometimes forgot to thank Allah for the real world around him. Akhlaq smiled and looked toward the rain-dark windows. The compass stayed still, but a small paper tab slipped out from beneath it: THE FIRST QUESTION IS NOT WHAT SHINES, BUT WHO CREATED IT.

At the door, Sheikh Uncle gave the children a rule. Nothing they learned would allow them to claim that they had visited the past, seen a Prophet, or heard speech that Allah had not preserved in revelation. The compass and story cards were ordinary teaching aids; the Qur’anic accounts were the truth to study. ‘Then why the mystery?’ Akhlaq asked. Sheikh Uncle closed the case. ‘Because curiosity can lead you either toward invention or toward knowledge. We are going to choose knowledge.’

stories.title: A Father's Question
stories.subtitle: Gentle speech, firm conviction, and respectful boundaries

blocks.text: The following afternoon, Akhlaq arrived at the library carrying a question he had been saving. ‘What if the person you disagree with is someone you love?’ Imaan explained that a classmate had wanted her to repeat a rumour about a teacher. She had refused, but afterward she kept wondering whether refusing a friend always had to sound rude. Sheikh Uncle opened the Qur’an to Sūrat Maryam, where Ibrāhīm addressed his father with repeated words of tenderness even as he challenged false worship.

Dadi Jaan pointed out that Ibrāhīm's kindness did not make his message less clear. He called his father away from worship that could neither hear nor see nor benefit him. His father rejected the invitation and threatened him. Ibrāhīm responded with a peaceful farewell and maintained distance from the wrongdoing. The lesson was not that children should obey harmful instructions. It was that good speech and firm principles can belong together.

Sheikh Uncle placed two cards beside the compass. One read: BE RIGHT AND BE CRUEL. The other read: BE KIND AND SAY NOTHING. ‘Are these the only choices?’ he asked. Imaan shook her head. Akhlaq thought about how he had answered his cousin that morning when the cousin had mocked a smaller child. ‘I told him he was a terrible person,’ he admitted. ‘Did he stop?’ Dadi asked. ‘No. We argued about my words instead.’

They practised another sentence: ‘Please don’t speak about him like that. It hurts, and we can stop.’ It was clear without humiliation. Sheikh Uncle explained that the example from Ibrāhīm's life involved a Prophet conveying revelation and must not be flattened into a classroom disagreement. Still, his respectful manner offered a principle worth applying to ordinary speech. Akhlaq placed the card marked BE RIGHT AND BE CRUEL face down. ‘That one fooled me,’ he admitted.

As they left, Imaan noticed a symbol etched on the compass: a small crescent beside the next mark. The attached instruction said, ‘A gentle voice can carry a difficult truth.’ Akhlaq looked up at the evening sky. ‘Are the stars our next clue?’ ‘Tomorrow,’ said Dadi, ‘we will learn why even the greatest light in the sky cannot be Allah.’

stories.title: When the Great Light Disappeared
stories.subtitle: The stars, moon, and sun are signs, not objects of worship

blocks.text: Sir Zameer had arranged a small astronomy evening on the school roof. Parents supervised, safety lamps marked the edges, and a teacher had brought a telescope. Akhlaq wanted to find the brightest object immediately. Mohsina wanted to know how the telescope worked. Imaan carried the compass case and a notebook titled THE THINGS WE KNOW. The air was still warm, and one bright point had become visible above the roofs.

Sir Zameer recited and explained the passage in Sūrat al-Anʿām about Ibrāhīm's argument involving a star, the moon and the sun. He explained that classical commentators discuss its argumentative context and that the account should not simply be staged as Ibrāhīm experimenting with different gods because he could not decide Whom to worship. His conclusion is clear: worship belongs to the Creator of the heavens and earth, not to created bodies that appear and set.

The younger children recorded the changing sky. The bright point disappeared from view. Later the moon shifted across the horizon. Everyone knew that the sun would rise and set as well. Akhlaq said, ‘Something can be huge and still depend on laws Allah created.’ Imaan added, ‘And the things Allah makes can remind us of Him without becoming things we worship.’ Sir Zameer nodded. The lesson did not ask children to stop learning astronomy. Rather, understanding the creation could deepen gratitude to its Creator.

Akhlaq was tempted to announce that he knew everything about the sky. Mohsina quietly asked him what the star was called. He paused. ‘I need to check,’ he admitted, remembering the Idrīs world. Sir Zameer praised the correction rather than the guess. Later, when a younger child asked whether a meteor was dangerous, he told the group that factual questions should be answered with evidence and safety advice, not frightening inventions.

Imaan wrote the next clue beneath the compass symbol: ADMIRE THE LIGHT. WORSHIP THE CREATOR. Akhlaq added a second line: WHEN I DO NOT KNOW, I WILL LEARN. Their lessons from earlier Prophets were beginning to meet one another, like pieces of a map that could not be completed by a single story.

stories.title: The Silent Hall
stories.subtitle: False worship, evidence, and the courage to accept correction

blocks.text: The school exhibition had an unusual table. Instead of prizes or trophies, Sir Zameer displayed photographs of historical objects and a simple worksheet: WHAT CAN THIS OBJECT DO? Some pictures showed carved figures, others showed tools, bowls and toys. The children were not asked to use any object for worship or to play at ancient religious rituals. The purpose was to understand the Qur’anic account of Ibrāhīm's challenge to idols made by human hands.

Sir Zameer narrated the established sequence from Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ: Ibrāhīm challenged his people's inherited practices; later, after the idols had been broken and the largest left, his argument exposed the helplessness of the things they worshipped. The Qur’an preserves the confrontation and the people's moment of recognition. It does not authorize teachers to invent additional conversations, architectural layouts, or acts for children to perform. The class studied the words in the Qur’an instead of acting out a Prophet's life.

Akhlaq pointed to a cracked clay cup and asked whether people could become attached to things that did not deserve that importance. ‘Of course,’ said Mohsin. ‘You became attached to the idea that your science project was perfect.’ Akhlaq protested. His bridge had won a small award. But when they examined it, its measurements were wrong. The teacher had corrected him the day before, and Akhlaq had refused to listen. Now he looked at his drawing and saw the faulty calculation clearly.

‘It is uncomfortable to discover that something you defended was wrong,’ Imaan said. The words were gentle enough that Akhlaq could hear them. He erased the measurement and began again. Sir Zameer explained that the historical story was about Tawḥīd and rejection of false worship, not merely accepting corrections in homework. Nevertheless, one small habit could help the heart: admit a mistake when the evidence is clear instead of becoming angry at the person who shows it.

At the end of the exhibition, the compass case contained a paper triangle with the words: THE TRUTH DOES NOT BECOME FALSE BECAUSE WE DISLIKE IT. Akhlaq carefully put his corrected drawing in his bag. For the first time that day, the revised page pleased him more than the trophy.

stories.title: The Crowd and the Fire
stories.subtitle: Steadfast faith and the miracle of Allah’s protection

blocks.text: One morning, the academy's message board filled with cruel jokes about a younger student. An older group had chosen him as the subject of a prank, and several children were repeating the messages without knowing what had happened. Akhlaq read them and felt the familiar pull of a crowd: when everyone laughed, saying nothing seemed easier. Imaan refused to share the messages. Mohsina suggested reporting the bullying to a trusted teacher rather than confronting the whole group alone.

That afternoon, Dadi Jaan read the Qur'anic account of the people who threatened Ibrāhīm with fire. They believed their numbers and power could silence the truth. But Allah commanded the fire to be coolness and safety for Ibrāhīm, and their plot failed. Dadi reminded everyone that this was a special miracle by Allah, not an invitation for children to take physical risks or expect miracles if they enter danger.

Akhlaq looked at the messages he had received. ‘So being brave does not mean running into trouble to prove I am brave.’ Exactly, Salaam said. Moral courage can mean refusing to join cruelty, preserving evidence, telling a responsible adult, or supporting someone safely. It may feel small compared with a great historical trial, but it can still be the right response in a child's world. Neither the children nor any app character would attempt to recreate the fire from the account.

Together, the children wrote to Sir Zameer about the bullying. The school acted without revealing who had reported it. The younger student found a kind note on his desk the next morning. He did not know who had written it, and that was fine. Akhlaq felt an unfamiliar relief: he had done something useful without winning an argument or gaining applause.

Dadi Jaan placed another compass card on the shelf. It read, COURAGE IS NOT CONTROL OVER THE ENDING. Akhlaq thought about Ibrāhīm's unwavering loyalty to Allah and the extraordinary rescue that only Allah could bring. Then he thought about the school corridor. One lesson belonged to divine history; the other belonged to a child's ordinary duty. Both pointed him away from following a crowd simply because it was powerful.

blocks.text: Faith and safe moral courage

stories.title: The King, the Sun, and a Question
stories.subtitle: Authority has limits; seeking reassurance with knowledge

blocks.text: Sheikh Uncle placed a small lamp beside a globe and challenged Akhlaq to make the sun rise from the west. Akhlaq could turn the globe and reverse the position of the light, of course, but Sheikh Uncle asked whether that changed the actual sun's course. The children laughed at the difference between a model and reality. Then the older teacher opened Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:258, where Ibrāhīm's debate exposed the limits of a ruler who disputed about Allah.

The Qur’an does not identify the ruler by name in that verse. Scholars record historical identifications, but a children's lesson should not turn those into unquestioned revelation. The essential point is that political power and confident speech do not create divine power. Ibrāhīm's argument about sunrise left the ruler without an answer. ‘Having an audience who agrees with you does not make your claim true,’ said Imaan. Mohsin remembered a class project in which he had claimed responsibility for work completed by the entire team.

Akhlaq then noticed the next passage in the workbook: 2:260. Ibrāhīm asked Allah to show him how He gives life to the dead. The answer in the verse makes clear that he already believed and sought reassurance for his heart. The instruction involving four birds belongs to a divine miracle; the activity did not invite the children to imitate it. Instead, they opened a question board where every student could write something they did not understand.

Imaan asked how to tell a sincere question from an argument designed only to win. Sheikh Uncle replied that a sincere learner listens, examines evidence and accepts correction. A person may ask more than once, but must not pretend a clear answer has not been given simply because it is inconvenient. Akhlaq submitted a question he had been embarrassed to ask in science class. When Sir Zameer gave a careful explanation, he listened and thanked him.

The compass showed two adjacent marks, one for humility before Allah's power and one for learning with an open heart. On the back, Sheikh Uncle had written: QUESTIONS CAN OPEN THE DOOR TO KNOWLEDGE. PRIDE CAN CLOSE IT.

stories.title: The Road Beyond the Familiar
stories.subtitle: Migration, trust, and choosing principle over comfort

blocks.text: The children were preparing for a community volunteering day when an unexpected message arrived. The activity had been moved from the school's comfortable indoor hall to a smaller centre across town, where the people most in need of help could actually attend. Akhlaq protested immediately. Their presentation screen would not fit. Their carefully arranged chairs would not be available. Even the snacks would change. ‘Why do we have to leave a perfectly good place?’ he asked.

On the way, Salamah reminded him of Ibrāhīm's declaration that he was going toward his Lord, trusting Allah to guide him. The Qur’an also tells us that Lūṭ believed him. His departure was part of his obedience and mission, not a game about adventure or a claim that every modern move is equivalent to Prophetic migration. The family did not attempt to invent the exact ancient roads, towns or dates that revelation leaves unreported.

At the new venue, the children noticed that their smaller presentation had something the old one did not: people could reach it easily. A child with a mobility aid could move comfortably between the tables. Parents asked questions without needing to travel far. Akhlaq felt his complaint grow smaller. The change had cost convenience, but had allowed the project to fulfil its purpose.

Imaan explained that choosing a difficult but right course often asks for patience after the decision. It is not enough to congratulate yourself for taking one step if you refuse to do the work that follows. Mohsina unpacked supplies. Mohsin carried boxes from the vehicle. Akhlaq helped make the tables accessible and finally admitted that their original plan had centred too much on their own comfort.

When they returned home, the compass clue read: A GOOD ROAD IS NOT ALWAYS THE EASIEST ROAD. Dadi Jaan asked them where its final destination should be. ‘Toward what is right,’ Imaan said. ‘And toward Allah's guidance,’ added Akhlaq.

blocks.text: Reliance and prioritizing what is right

stories.title: The Valley and the Water
stories.subtitle: Hājar’s effort, Zamzam, and trust with responsible action

blocks.text: Dadi Jaan spread a blank paper across the table and asked the children to draw a valley without houses or gardens. Akhlaq added mountains, a small path and nothing else. ‘It looks lonely,’ he said. Dadi explained that the Qur’an records Ibrāhīm's supplication after settling some of his family near Allah's Sacred House in an uncultivated valley. An authentic narration in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3364 provides further details about Hājar, her infant Ismāʿīl and the coming of Zamzam.

The story was told carefully. Hājar trusted Allah, yet she did not sit idle when water was needed. She moved between Ṣafā and Marwah seeking help and provision. Allah granted relief through Zamzam. Dadi made sure the children understood that this was a particular account within revelation and authentic Sunnah, not a reason to imagine that parents may abandon children or that every hardship will end with a visible miracle.

Akhlaq leaned over the paper valley. ‘She trusted Allah and she acted.’ Salaam agreed. Tawakkul is not carelessness: in ordinary life, a child who needs help must tell a trusted adult, follow safety guidance and take the responsible steps available. The family discussed how people today can run short of safe drinking water through no wrongdoing of their own. They agreed to help a local approved relief project, with adults handling the money and arrangements.

Imaan drew a blue circle in her notebook and marked it ZAMZAM. Mohsina drew a second beside it and labelled it OUR RESPONSIBILITY. The two circles were not being equated: one recalled a blessed historic event, the other a present-day act of care. Akhlaq cut out small paper cups to remind the group to serve water without waste.

Later, while sorting materials, they discovered another folded compass card: TRUST IS NOT THE OPPOSITE OF EFFORT. Sheikh Uncle had chosen the words deliberately. The children would carry them into the next episode, where welcoming others would become an important lesson.

stories.title: Guests, Glad Tidings, and a Gentle Welcome
stories.subtitle: Hospitality, humility, and trust in Allah’s promise

blocks.text: The community centre was preparing to receive visiting families when Imaan and Akhlaq discovered that the welcome table was completely empty. Someone had delivered the chairs but forgotten the water jug and name cards. Instead of complaining, they began putting things right. Mohsina carried clean cups, and Mohsin checked that the entrance was open and easy to use. Akhlaq wanted to make an elaborate display but Imaan pointed out that the guests first needed a comfortable place to sit.

That evening, Sheikh Uncle read the passage about the honoured visitors who came to Ibrāhīm. The Qur’an describes his generous response and the meal he offered. When his guests did not eat, he became apprehensive; they reassured him and brought news that belonged to Allah's promise. The scholars explain the guests as angels, but the children would not draw or act them as ordinary game characters. The episode's purpose was learning hospitality and recalling the authentic good news, not inventing what the visitors looked like.

Dadi Jaan explained that the glad tidings concerning Isḥāq and the blessing of his family were not a general promise that every worried person will receive exactly what they want. Allah's power and wisdom belong to Him. The children could learn to greet guests kindly, offer appropriate refreshment, and speak gently without imagining that they had control over the unseen.

When the visitors arrived at the community centre, Akhlaq watched a shy younger child stand apart from the group. He resisted the urge to ask a dozen questions and simply offered a seat near the activity table. Imaan spoke to the child's parent and asked what would make the visit easier. The guests began to relax, and the centre filled with comfortable conversation rather than noise and boasting.

At home, the compass clue said: THE BEAUTY OF WELCOME IS IN HOW OTHERS FEEL, NOT HOW IMPRESSIVE YOU APPEAR. Akhlaq remembered the towers his team had built in the Hūd world. There was nothing wrong with a beautiful welcome table, but kindness mattered more than admiration.

stories.title: The Hardest Trust
stories.subtitle: Obedience, the great test, mercy, and safe ethical application

blocks.text: The morning before Eid al-Aḍḥā, the children helped organise small gift parcels for a family-support programme. Akhlaq was eager to fill every parcel with the same items, but Imaan asked whether every family needed the same things. Salamah explained that respecting people meant listening to their needs without asking them to disclose private difficulties in public. The work had to be thoughtful, not merely impressive.

After the parcels were ready, Dadi Jaan introduced the most difficult passage in their Ibrāhīm learning journey: the vision and the great test described in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt 37:102–107. She explained it with age-sensitive language. Ibrāhīm received an extraordinary command in a Prophetic dream, the son responded with submission, and Allah provided a ransom before the sacrifice could occur. Neither was this an invitation for ordinary people to act on dreams, nor could children imitate the story with pretend weapons, violence, or frightening challenges.

‘So what is our action?’ Akhlaq asked. ‘Are we meant to give something up?’ Dadi replied that they could learn obedience to Allah within the duties actually prescribed for them: truthfulness, care for family, kindness to animals, prayer, and generosity. They must never hurt themselves or anyone else as a supposed test of faith. The scholars commonly identify the son as Ismāʿīl, while the particular verses do not explicitly name him; that distinction would appear in the evidence notes.

Imaan suggested that their real challenge should be to give up some personal convenience to help someone respectfully. Mohsin agreed to spend time packing and carrying supplies rather than playing a game at home. Akhlaq began with reluctance and soon found the work more satisfying than he had expected. They did not call their choice a sacrifice comparable to Ibrāhīm's trial. It was a small, ordinary act of service learned from a sacred account.

In the evening the compass showed the words: THE TEST OF FAITH DOES NOT GIVE US PERMISSION TO HARM. Allah's mercy and guidance remained central to the story. The children closed their books with gratitude and a clear understanding that a game must never turn this account into an action challenge involving injury.

stories.title: Raise the Foundations
stories.subtitle: The Kaʿbah, duʿāʾ, and working sincerely with family

blocks.text: Sheikh Uncle opened an atlas and showed the children a photograph of the Kaʿbah, then read Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:127. Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl raised the foundations of the House and prayed for Allah to accept their work. Their supplication amazed Akhlaq: even while doing something great, they asked for acceptance. The children had expected a triumphant speech. Instead, they learned humility.

For the next community-centre event, the children were asked to prepare a reading corner. Mohsina made a list of books, Imaan designed quiet spaces for readers, Mohsin assembled safe shelves under adult supervision, and Akhlaq prepared the labels. When he had finished his part, he wanted to hang a large notice saying that he had organised everything. Imaan gently reminded him that four people had worked, and many adults had helped too.

Salaam spoke about the danger of making goodness depend on applause. The House raised by Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl was not a trophy for human fame; it was connected to worship of Allah. Our modest reading corner, he said, was not comparable to that sacred construction, but we could still remember to serve sincerely, thank helpers and ask Allah for acceptance. Akhlaq changed the sign to say: EVERYONE IS WELCOME TO READ.

Dadi Jaan then taught the children the supplication, ‘Our Lord, accept from us,’ as contained within the verse. They practised it with correct Arabic pronunciation using approved recitation, and reviewed the difference between a Qur’anic duʿāʾ and a phrase invented for their class activity. The app would show the complete verse alongside any memorisation segment so the words would not be detached from context.

When the first visitors arrived, the children showed them the books without boasting. One little boy selected a story and settled on the carpet with a smile. Akhlaq watched him and whispered, ‘That is enough.’ The compass card for this episode read: WORK WELL. ASK ALLAH TO ACCEPT.

stories.title: What the Compass Was Pointing To
stories.subtitle: The legacy of Ibrāhīm and the bridge to the next Prophetic world

blocks.text: There was one mark left on the compass. Eleven had been filled with tiny paper symbols: a book, a hand, a star, an empty display, a flame, a sunrise, a question, a road, a water drop, a cup, and a simple square. Akhlaq inspected the back for the secret panel he was sure existed. Sheikh Uncle laughed and told him that the answer was inside the children's notebooks. Every mark represented an important Qur’anic lesson they had studied, not a magical door or a hidden historical place.

The family and their friends gathered around the library table for a final exhibition. Mohsina explained the difference between a verse of the Qur’an and a story written to apply its guidance. Imaan presented the reminder about gentle speech to family members. Mohsin spoke about using strength in service. Akhlaq placed their astronomy drawing beside the corrected science-project diagram and explained why truth should not depend on which person was loudest or most popular.

Sheikh Uncle opened Sūrat al-Naḥl, which praises Ibrāhīm for devoted obedience, gratitude and freedom from shirk. They reviewed the true foundation: worship Allah alone and follow the guidance revealed through His Messengers. His life is not a collection of impressive episodes with unrelated moral slogans; the faith that united them gave direction to each action. Children could admire his courage, patience, hospitality and gratitude without pretending to possess his Prophetic role or reenacting miracles.

‘So where was the treasure?’ Akhlaq asked. Dadi Jaan placed a plain card at the centre of the compass: THE WAY YOU CHOOSE TO LIVE AFTER LEARNING. It was not an ancient quotation and never claimed to be. It was the family's summary of their task: to respond to revelation with understanding, humility and appropriate action. The final mark was complete.

Sheikh Uncle returned the compass to its case but did not lock the box. ‘It belongs to the learning library now,’ he said. ‘Other children will use it, and we will tell them what is real and what is our teaching story.’ Imaan noticed a new envelope beside it. On the front was written: LŪṬ — SPEAKING THE TRUTH WITH COURAGE. She smiled. The journey was continuing, but it would continue one carefully sourced chapter at a time.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND
discover.text: AGE-APPROPRIATE TAFSĪR & CONTEXT

Allah gave Ibrāhīm sound guidance and knowledge, and the Qurʾān records his challenge to the idol worship of his people. This is first a lesson about Tawḥīd, not merely a lesson about treating objects carefully. The people defended worship inherited from earlier generations, but the Prophet asked why they relied on things unable to hear or independently help. Ibn Kathīr and other classical exegetes read these passages as a direct challenge to shirk and inherited error. Children must understand that respecting a tool or admiring a human achievement is different from worship. The created world is full of gifts and signs, but only Allah is the Creator, Sustainer and One worthy of worship.

Akhlaq proudly announces that his new robot can “do anything.” Imaan asks whether it can make itself, choose its own purpose, or work without electricity. Akhlaq laughs at his exaggeration and thanks Allah for the ability to learn.

فَلَمَّا بَلَغَ مَعَهُ ٱلسَّعْىَ قَالَ يَـٰبُنَىَّ إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰ فِى ٱلْمَنَامِ أَنِّىٓ أَذْبَحُكَ فَٱنظُرْ مَاذَا تَرَىٰ ۚ قَالَ يَـٰٓأَبَتِ ٱفْعَلْ مَا تُؤْمَرُ ۖ سَتَجِدُنِىٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّـٰبِرِينَ
Meaning guide (37:102): The son had reached the age of working alongside Ibrāhīm when the Prophetic vision of sacrifice became a great test.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND
discover.text: AGE-APPROPRIATE TAFSĪR & CONTEXT

The Qurʾān recounts a profound test shown to Ibrāhīm in a Prophetic dream. The son responded obediently; before the intended sacrifice occurred, Allah provided a great ransom and declared the test fulfilled. In the passage the son is not named explicitly; classical exegetes commonly identify him as Ismāʿīl. The account teaches submission to Allah and His mercy. It is never permission for an ordinary adult or child to follow a dream commanding harm. The user interface must never show tools of violence or demand imitation. Contemporary good deeds must follow what Allah has actually prescribed and what is safe, voluntary and respectful.
DECIDE — FICTIONAL IMAAN & AKHLAQ SITUATION
Before Eid al-Aḍḥā, the children pack family-support gifts. Akhlaq volunteers some leisure time so the parcels can be finished with care.

missions.question: What is a safe daily lesson from this sacred test?

choices.text: Choose an ordinary good deed and obey Allah’s established guidance.
choices.feedback: Correct. We learn obedience and mercy, not dangerous imitation.

choices.text: Believe anyone who claims a dream permits harm.
choices.feedback: Dream claims do not allow harm to others.

وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمُ ٱلْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَـٰعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ
Meaning guide (2:127): Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl raised the foundations of the House and asked Allah to accept from them.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND
discover.text: AGE-APPROPRIATE TAFSĪR & CONTEXT

Allah recalls Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl raising the foundations of the House while supplicating, “Our Lord, accept from us.” Their work belongs to sacred history linked to Tawḥīd and worship; it is not merely a lesson about building an ordinary structure. The children can recognise teamwork, gratitude and sincerity as practical applications, but must not confuse their craft projects with the Kaʿbah or turn the Kaʿbah into a collectible treasure. The Arabic duʿāʾ should be taught from the complete verified verse, with authentic recitation and age-appropriate translation. The precise geometry and original stones of the historical construction should not be invented.
DECIDE — FICTIONAL IMAAN & AKHLAQ SITUATION

رَبِّ ٱجْعَلْنِى مُقِيمَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةِ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِى ۚ رَبَّنَا وَتَقَبَّلْ دُعَآءِ
Meaning guide (14:40): Ibrāhīm asked Allah to make him and his descendants steadfast in prayer and to accept his supplication.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND
discover.text: AGE-APPROPRIATE TAFSĪR & CONTEXT

Ibrāhīm prayed for safety from idolatry, for his children, and for establishment of prayer. The Qurʾān teaches that a family’s deepest welfare is not merely comfort and status but sound belief and sincere worship. The Prophet’s personal supplications are preserved in revelation; their wording must be kept accurate and not paraphrased as if a new duʿāʾ were a Qurʾānic verse. A child can learn to ask Allah for help in Salah and to contribute to a peaceful home through small acts of care. Teachers must be gentle toward children whose family circumstances differ from the ideal or who lack supportive caregivers.
DECIDE — FICTIONAL IMAAN & AKHLAQ SITUATION
Imaan proposes a small family prayer reminder, while Akhlaq asks if a reminder should ever embarrass someone who is learning slowly. Dadi recommends gentleness.

choices.text: Offer a kind reminder and ask how you can help.
choices.feedback: Yes. Help and patience make guidance easier to receive.

choices.text: Announce that they will never improve.
choices.feedback: Never define a learner by an early difficulty.

missions.title: The Friend of Allah: A Lasting Legacy

discover.text: Linked story 12 | Main āyah 16:120 | Supporting: Al-Naḥl 16:120–123; Al-Nisāʾ 4:125; Al-Baqarah 2:124

discover.label: TARGET / MASTERY
discover.text: Faith, gratitude and consistency — Recall the qualities with which the Qurʾān praises Ibrāhīm and identify one personal habit to carry forward.

discover.label: READ
discover.text: COMPLETE SELECTED QURʾĀNIC ĀYAH
إِنَّ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ كَانَ أُمَّةً قَانِتًا لِّلَّهِ حَنِيفًا وَلَمْ يَكُ مِنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ
Meaning guide (16:120): Allah praises Ibrāhīm as an exemplary upright servant, devoted to Him and free from shirk.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND
discover.text: AGE-APPROPRIATE TAFSĪR & CONTEXT

The Qurʾān praises Ibrāhīm as devoted, upright, grateful and not among those who associated partners with Allah. It also identifies him with the honour of Allah’s close friendship and leadership for people. These qualities are not arbitrary tokens or points; they belong to Allah’s description of His Messenger. Across the volume, children have learned that Tawḥīd gives direction to courage, hospitality, patience, effort and prayer. Their task now is to carry a small, honest habit into daily life, remembering that their own spiritual status is not something an app can measure. Completion means demonstrating understanding and choosing appropriate action, not receiving a ranking in piety.
DECIDE — FICTIONAL IMAAN & AKHLAQ SITUATION
The children arrange their compass clues on the library table, distinguish revealed history from fictional examples and agree to help younger learners with the next world.

choices.text: That learning should lead to worship, humility and good actions.
choices.feedback: Correct. Guidance is meant to shape life beyond the screen.

choices.text: That the stories give us special powers.
choices.feedback: The compass is a learning tool, not a magical object.

review.arabic: وَإِذْ جَعَلْنَا ٱلْبَيْتَ مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا وَٱتَّخِذُوا۟ مِن مَّقَامِ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمَ مُصَلًّى ۖ وَعَهِدْنَآ إِلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمَ وَإِسْمَـٰعِيلَ أَن طَهِّرَا بَيْتِىَ لِلطَّآئِفِينَ وَٱلْعَـٰكِفِينَ وَٱلرُّكَّعِ ٱلسُّجُودِ
review.meaning: Allah recalled His House as a place for people and commanded its purification for worship.

review.arabic: وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمُ ٱلْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَـٰعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl raised the foundations of the House and asked Allah to accept from them.

review.arabic: رَبَّنَا وَٱجْعَلْنَا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةً مُّسْلِمَةً لَّكَ وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا وَتُبْ عَلَيْنَآ ۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
review.meaning: They prayed to be submissive to Allah and for guidance in acts of worship.

review.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى ٱلَّذِى حَآجَّ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمَ فِى رَبِّهِۦٓ أَنْ ءَاتَىٰهُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمُلْكَ إِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّىَ ٱلَّذِى يُحْىِۦ وَيُمِيتُ قَالَ أَنَا۠ أُحْىِۦ وَأُمِيتُ ۖ قَالَ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمُ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْتِى بِٱلشَّمْسِ مِنَ ٱلْمَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِهَا مِنَ ٱلْمَغْرِبِ فَبُهِتَ ٱلَّذِى كَفَرَ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهْدِى ٱلْقَوْمَ ٱلظَّـٰلِمِينَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm confronted a ruler’s argument about Allah with the challenge concerning the rising of the sun.

review.arabic: وَإِذْ قَالَ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ أَرِنِى كَيْفَ تُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ ۖ قَالَ أَوَلَمْ تُؤْمِن ۖ قَالَ بَلَىٰ وَلَـٰكِن لِّيَطْمَئِنَّ قَلْبِى ۖ قَالَ فَخُذْ أَرْبَعَةً مِّنَ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَصُرْهُنَّ إِلَيْكَ ثُمَّ ٱجْعَلْ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ جَبَلٍ مِّنْهُنَّ جُزْءًا ثُمَّ ٱدْعُهُنَّ يَأْتِينَكَ سَعْيًا ۚ وَٱعْلَمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm sought reassurance by asking Allah to show him how He gives life to the dead; Allah instructed him concerning four birds.

review.arabic: وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ دِينًا مِّمَّنْ أَسْلَمَ وَجْهَهُۥ لِلَّهِ وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ وَٱتَّبَعَ مِلَّةَ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ حَنِيفًا ۗ وَٱتَّخَذَ ٱللَّهُ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ خَلِيلًا
review.meaning: Allah states that He took Ibrāhīm as an intimate friend.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلَّيْلُ رَءَا كَوْكَبًا ۖ قَالَ هَـٰذَا رَبِّى ۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَ قَالَ لَآ أُحِبُّ ٱلْءَافِلِينَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm used the star’s disappearance in his argument against false worship.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّا رَءَا ٱلشَّمْسَ بَازِغَةً قَالَ هَـٰذَا رَبِّى هَـٰذَآ أَكْبَرُ ۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَتْ قَالَ يَـٰقَوْمِ إِنِّى بَرِىٓءٌ مِّمَّا تُشْرِكُونَ
review.meaning: The rising and setting of the sun formed part of his argument about created things.

review.arabic: إِنِّى وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِىَ لِلَّذِى فَطَرَ ٱلسَّمَـٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ حَنِيفًا ۖ وَمَآ أَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm declared that he turned his face toward the Creator of the heavens and earth as an upright worshipper.

review.arabic: رَّبَّنَآ إِنِّىٓ أَسْكَنتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِى بِوَادٍ غَيْرِ ذِى زَرْعٍ عِندَ بَيْتِكَ ٱلْمُحَرَّمِ رَبَّنَا لِيُقِيمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ فَٱجْعَلْ أَفْـِٔدَةً مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ تَهْوِىٓ إِلَيْهِمْ وَٱرْزُقْهُم مِّنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَشْكُرُونَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm prayed concerning his descendants settled in an uncultivated valley by the Sacred House, seeking worship and provision.

review.arabic: رَبِّ ٱجْعَلْنِى مُقِيمَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةِ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِى ۚ رَبَّنَا وَتَقَبَّلْ دُعَآءِ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm asked Allah to make him and his descendants steadfast in prayer and to accept his supplication.

review.arabic: قَالُوا۟ لَا تَوْجَلْ إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَـٰمٍ عَلِيمٍ
review.meaning: The visitors reassured Ibrāhīm and conveyed good news about a knowledgeable son.

review.arabic: قَالَ وَمَن يَقْنَطُ مِن رَّحْمَةِ رَبِّهِۦٓ إِلَّا ٱلضَّآلُّونَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm affirmed hope in Allah’s mercy.

review.arabic: إِنَّ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ كَانَ أُمَّةً قَانِتًا لِّلَّهِ حَنِيفًا وَلَمْ يَكُ مِنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ
review.meaning: Allah praises Ibrāhīm as an exemplary upright servant, devoted to Him and free from shirk.

review.arabic: شَاكِرًا لِّأَنْعُمِهِ ۚ ٱجْتَبَىٰهُ وَهَدَىٰهُ إِلَىٰ صِرَٰطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ
review.meaning: He was grateful for Allah’s blessings, and Allah chose and guided him.

review.arabic: إِذْ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ يَـٰٓأَبَتِ لِمَ تَعْبُدُ مَا لَا يَسْمَعُ وَلَا يُبْصِرُ وَلَا يُغْنِى عَنكَ شَيْـًٔا
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm respectfully asked his father why he worshipped what could not hear, see or benefit him.

review.arabic: قَالَ أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ ءَالِهَتِى يَـٰٓإِبْرَٰهِيمُ ۖ لَئِن لَّمْ تَنتَهِ لَأَرْجُمَنَّكَ ۖ وَٱهْجُرْنِى مَلِيًّا
review.meaning: His father rejected the invitation and threatened him.

review.arabic: قَالَ سَلَـٰمٌ عَلَيْكَ ۖ سَأَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكَ رَبِّىٓ ۖ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ بِى حَفِيًّا
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm replied peacefully and spoke of seeking forgiveness for his father.

review.arabic: وَلَقَدْ ءَاتَيْنَآ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ رُشْدَهُۥ مِن قَبْلُ وَكُنَّا بِهِۦ عَـٰلِمِينَ
review.meaning: Allah granted Ibrāhīm his sound guidance, and Allah knew him well.

review.arabic: إِذْ قَالَ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوْمِهِۦ مَا هَـٰذِهِ ٱلتَّمَاثِيلُ ٱلَّتِىٓ أَنتُمْ لَهَا عَـٰكِفُونَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm asked his father and people about the images to which they devoted themselves.

review.arabic: وَتَٱللَّهِ لَأَكِيدَنَّ أَصْنَـٰمَكُم بَعْدَ أَن تُوَلُّوا۟ مُدْبِرِينَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm declared his intention concerning their idols after they went away.

review.arabic: قَالَ بَلْ فَعَلَهُۥ كَبِيرُهُمْ هَـٰذَا فَسْـَٔلُوهُمْ إِن كَانُوا۟ يَنطِقُونَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm directed his people toward the largest idol as part of an argument exposing the inability of the idols to speak.

review.arabic: قَالَ أَفَتَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ مَا لَا يَنفَعُكُمْ شَيْـًٔا وَلَا يَضُرُّكُمْ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm challenged them for worshipping things besides Allah that could neither benefit nor harm them.

review.arabic: قَالُوا۟ حَرِّقُوهُ وَٱنصُرُوٓا۟ ءَالِهَتَكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ فَـٰعِلِينَ
review.meaning: His opponents called for burning Ibrāhīm in support of their false objects of worship.

review.arabic: قُلْنَا يَـٰنَارُ كُونِى بَرْدًا وَسَلَـٰمًا عَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ
review.meaning: Allah commanded the fire to be coolness and safety for Ibrāhīm.

review.arabic: وَأَرَادُوا۟ بِهِۦ كَيْدًا فَجَعَلْنَـٰهُمُ ٱلْأَخْسَرِينَ
review.meaning: Their plot against Ibrāhīm failed by Allah’s decree.

review.arabic: فَـَٔامَنَ لَهُۥ لُوطٌ ۘ وَقَالَ إِنِّى مُهَاجِرٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّىٓ ۖ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ
review.meaning: Lūṭ believed him; Ibrāhīm declared his departure in devotion to his Lord.

review.arabic: وَقَالَ إِنِّى ذَاهِبٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّى سَيَهْدِينِ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm said he was going to his Lord, who would guide him.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّا بَلَغَ مَعَهُ ٱلسَّعْىَ قَالَ يَـٰبُنَىَّ إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰ فِى ٱلْمَنَامِ أَنِّىٓ أَذْبَحُكَ فَٱنظُرْ مَاذَا تَرَىٰ ۚ قَالَ يَـٰٓأَبَتِ ٱفْعَلْ مَا تُؤْمَرُ ۖ سَتَجِدُنِىٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّـٰبِرِينَ
review.meaning: The son had reached the age of working alongside Ibrāhīm when the Prophetic vision of sacrifice became a great test.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّآ أَسْلَمَا وَتَلَّهُۥ لِلْجَبِينِ
review.meaning: They submitted to Allah’s command in this extraordinary test.

review.arabic: وَنَـٰدَيْنَـٰهُ أَن يَـٰٓإِبْرَٰهِيمُ
review.meaning: Allah called out to Ibrāhīm.

review.arabic: قَدْ صَدَّقْتَ ٱلرُّءْيَآ ۚ إِنَّا كَذَٰلِكَ نَجْزِى ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ
review.meaning: Allah declared that the vision had been fulfilled and the devoted were rewarded.

review.arabic: إِنَّ هَـٰذَا لَهُوَ ٱلْبَلَـٰٓؤُا۟ ٱلْمُبِينُ

review.arabic: وَفَدَيْنَـٰهُ بِذِبْحٍ عَظِيمٍ

review.arabic: هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ ٱلْمُكْرَمِينَ
review.meaning: The account introduces the honoured guests of Ibrāhīm.

review.arabic: فَرَاغَ إِلَىٰٓ أَهْلِهِۦ فَجَآءَ بِعِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm prepared a generous meal for his guests.

synthesis.text: The journey begins with Tawḥīd. Every event in the story of Ibrāhīm is connected to his devotion to Allah alone. He challenged inherited false worship, spoke to his father with respectful clarity, showed why the stars and sun could not be gods, exposed the helplessness of idols, and held fast to his calling when human power threatened him. His conviction did not arise from popularity, wealth or control of other people. It rested upon the guidance of Allah.

The same faith shaped his trust. In the Qurʾānic account he confronted a ruler’s pretensions, sought reassurance from Allah with a believing heart, and left what was familiar in obedience to his Lord. Hājar’s effort, established through authentic Sunnah, reminds the learner that trust and responsible action are not opposites. Hospitality, gratitude, and hope appear alongside hardship and uncertainty. The great test of sacrifice shows submission and mercy but cannot be replicated as a child’s physical challenge.

When Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl raised the foundations of the Kaʿbah, their supplication asked Allah for acceptance. This brings the entire journey together: the best deeds need sincerity. A child may receive marks, compliments and game achievements, but no digital reward can establish their spiritual rank before Allah. A mission is complete when the learner has understood a source, reflected on it, and been offered a safe way to practise one relevant good deed.

In the fictional children’s story, the compass was never magical. Its marks represented learning. Imaan and Akhlaq discovered that curiosity must be disciplined by evidence, courage by responsibility, knowledge by humility, and generosity by respect. The same habits can travel with them into the next world, long after the screen is closed.
